An Expensive Reckoning is Coming for Apartment Owners
 
Plus, expiring tax breaks pressure New York City residential buildings
 
By Craig Karmin
 

This is an edition of the Real Estate newsletter, a weekly briefing of the biggest commercial deals, news, analysis and trends in office, multifamily, retail and other commercial sectors. If you’re not subscribed, sign up here.

 

Nearly every property developer feels the pain from rising interest rates. Perhaps none more so than apartment landlords. These real estate owners face a bill of more than $1.8 trillion in debt over the next decade. From this year to 2028, about $757 billion of those loans are coming due, the most of any commercial real-estate sector.

 

Apartment rents surged when interest rates were at historic lows, and multifamily became a refuge for real-estate investors. Now mortgage rates are roughly double the rate of five years ago as these loans come due. “There was a sense of relative euphoria,” said Newmark’s Mike Wolfson. “But things turned very quickly.” Rebecca Picciotto explains how it all may shake out.

 

In New York City, meanwhile, expiring tax breaks are about to make the city even more expensive. Thousands of residential buildings are losing property tax abatements in the years ahead. Renters will feel the squeeze along with condo and co-op owners. Ginger Adams Otis talks to New Yorkers who are seeing their tax bills skyrocket as tax breaks offered developers decades ago to build new housing are now burning off.

 
 
 

Apartment Landlords Have a $2 Trillion Debt Problem That Is Only Getting Worse

 
 
ELIJAH NOUVELAGE/BLOOMBERG NEWS
 

Few investors are feeling more pain from rising interest rates than America’s apartment landlords.

 

These property owners face a bill of more than $1.8 trillion in debt over the next decade.

 
 
 
$757 billion
 

The amount of apartment loans coming due from this year to 2028, according to the Mortgage Bankers Association. Landlords are having to refinance when borrowing rates are roughly twice the level of five years ago, when many of these loans were made.

 
 
 

Expiring Property Tax Breaks Are About to Make New York Even More Expensive

 
 
LAILA ANNMARIE STEVENS FOR WSJ
 

When Derek MacKenzie moved into his Brooklyn condo in 2022, his annual property tax bill was $140. This year, it ballooned to $7,600. Next year it is projected to hit $10,500.

 

The surge in tax reflects the end of an abatement his Park Slope condo enjoyed for roughly 15 years.

 
 
 

Data Points

 

• $75 billion: U.S. data-center construction annualized spending, as of July, according to Savills. That is a nearly 60% year-over-year increase, and has helped boost warehouse leasing as data companies require more space for power and cooling infrastructure, equipment and other related services.

 

• 70%: The share of visits to bricks-and-mortar retailers lasting 30 minutes or less, according to Placer.ai, showing that most shopping is driven by convenience.
